newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile sees $1 bln non-metallic mining boom.
newsitem.headline: Chile sees $1 bln non-metallic mining boom.

text.p: Chile expects investment in the non-metallic mining industry to climb to $1 billion over the next five years with the country becoming the world's top iodine and lithium producer by the end of the decade, said an official.
"Non-metallic minerals currently account for just five percent of mining exports," said Vicente Perez, a researcher at state studies center Comision Chilena del Cobre.
"But we expect Chile to become world leader in iodine and lithium production in 2000."
In a country where copper is king, non-metallic minerals are beginning to emerge from the shadows of more tradition mining industry thanks to a wave of new projects in Chile's arid north.
The Atacama Desert, covered by the sea millions of years ago, is dotted with dry salt lakes rich in minerals ranging from nitrates to boric acid.
Cosayach, a company linked to Chile's Errazuriz group, is investing around $50 million to expand iodine output and move into nitrates at its property in the First Region, said Perez.
The firm will increase its iodine production from under 1,000 tonnes this year to 2,600 tonnes when the expansion is completed mid-1998. Nitrate production will be around 200,000 tonnes a year.
Other nitrate/iodine projects under construction include schemes being built by Canadian-owned Minera Yolanda and the $69 million Aguas Blancas project.
These investments will challenge fertilizer-maker Socidad Quimica y Minera de Chile's (Soquimich) traditional dominance of Chile's non-metallic market, said Perez.
